title: The questions it must answer
lede: A {{Competency question}} is an ordinary question the finished system has to be able to answer. They are written first, by people, and everything built afterwards is measured against them. This is the list — including the ones it cannot answer, which are the more informative half.

items.label: Need search or AI retrieval first
items.note: two stages that do not exist yet

items.label: Answered by refusing
items.note: CQ-0012 returns the things it must not say

blocks.title: One of them is answered by saying no
blocks.text: *Is the connotation in this trade mark strong enough to warrant a ground for rejection?* is an evaluative judgement for the decision maker. The system's answer is the list of outputs that would answer it and must never be produced. That is a designed behaviour, not a missing feature.

rows.question: What guidance does the Manual give on when a ground for rejection under section 43 should be raised?
rows.search: CQ-0001 What guidance does the Manual give on when a ground for rejection under section 43 should be raised? examiner

detail.text: **A good answer mentions:** *connotation*, *likely to deceive or cause confusion*, *ground for rejection*
**Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/1#1`
**May also cite:** `TMA1995/s43`, `TMM/Part29/2/2/4`, `TMM/Part29/3#1~1`

**What a good answer looks like.** Must state the statutory test in the words of s 43 and separately state the Manual's practice guidance, marked as practice rather than as law. Must convey that the section is mandatory in application while the threshold question — whether the decision maker is clearly satisfied — is an evaluative one.

detail.title: Where an answer can go wrong
detail.text: The Manual's own text quotes s 43 in full inside TMM/Part29/1#1, so an answer can appear to cite the Act while only having read the Manual. That is a grounding failure that will not show up as a missing source.

rows.question: My trade mark has a place name in it. Will that stop it being registered?
rows.search: CQ-0003 My trade mark has a place name in it. Will that stop it being registered? applicant

detail.text: **A good answer mentions:** *geographical reference*, *geographical origin*, *condition of registration*
**Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/9#1`, `TMM/Part29/9/9/3~1`
**May also cite:** `TMM/Part29/9/9/2`, `TMM/Part29/9/9/4`, `TMM/Part29/9/9/5`

**What a good answer looks like.** Must not answer yes or no. Must set out the criteria the Manual applies and state that the outcome depends on the specification and the surrounding circumstances, and must point to the route by which such a ground is overcome rather than leaving the applicant with a refusal.

detail.title: Where an answer can go wrong
detail.text: An answer that reads as advice on this applicant's mark has crossed from retrieval into an evaluative conclusion — see PU-0001.

rows.question: Where a trade mark contains an INN stem, what does the Manual say about raising section 43 alongside a ground under section 41 or section 44?
rows.search: CQ-0004 Where a trade mark contains an INN stem, what does the Manual say about raising section 43 alongside a ground under section 41 or section 44? examiner

detail.text: **A good answer mentions:** *International Non-Proprietary Name*, *INN stem*, *condition of registration*
**Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/5/5/4`

**What a good answer looks like.** Must state that the endorsement limiting use to goods containing the designated substance addresses the section 43 ground only, and must not imply that it disposes of a section 41 or section 44 ground.

detail.title: Where an answer can go wrong
detail.text: The Manual states this negatively — "unlikely to assist in overcoming grounds… raised for other reasons". A summariser will drop the negation.

rows.question: Where do I find the practice on celebrity names in trade marks?
rows.search: CQ-0005 Where do I find the practice on celebrity names in trade marks? examiner

detail.text: **A good answer mentions:** *well-known person*, *endorsement*, *written permission*
**Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/6#1~1`, `TMM/Part29/6#1~2`
**May also cite:** `TMM/Part29/6/6/1`, `TMM/Part29/6/6/2~1`

**What a good answer looks like.** Must reach Part 29.6 from a term Part 29.6 never uses. Ranking the deceased-persons material above the general material would be a wrong ordering rather than a wrong answer.

rows.question: Can I register a brand that uses a famous sportsperson's name if they have signed off on it?
rows.search: CQ-0006 Can I register a brand that uses a famous sportsperson's name if they have signed off on it? applicant

detail.text: **A good answer mentions:** *written permission*, *endorsement*
**Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/6#1~2`
**May also cite:** `TMM/Part29/6#1~1`

**What a good answer looks like.** Must surface the permission route and the endorsement wording, and must make clear that the endorsement is the Registrar's suggested form of words rather than a statutory requirement.

rows.question: Confusion between my mark and someone else's — which section is that?
rows.search: CQ-0007 Confusion between my mark and someone else's — which section is that? applicant

detail.text: **A good answer mentions:** *deceptively similar*, *connotation*
**Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/2/2/3`
**May also cite:** `TMA1995/s44`, `TMM/Part29/3/3/3`

**What a good answer looks like.** Must send the reader to section 44, and must say why section 43 is not the answer: a connotation arises from the mark itself, not from a comparison with another mark.

detail.title: Where an answer can go wrong
detail.text: This is the highest-frequency false positive in the pilot area. An answer that lands anywhere in Part 29.3 is wrong in a way that reads entirely plausibly.

detail.title: What the stored query does not establish
detail.text:
Answers by routing, not by deciding. The Manual allocates the comparison elsewhere and this returns the sentence that says so with its passage; it does not assess any mark. Note the concepts named in `notLabel` — the retrieval trap here is that both destinations are about confusion, so a match on the word alone sends an examiner to the wrong test (GX-0005).

Every stored query carries a line like this. A query that returns a neat table always looks like an answer, and this is where it says what it has not proved.

rows.question: Is "-profen" on the restricted list?
rows.search: CQ-0008 Is "-profen" on the restricted list? examiner

detail.text: **A good answer mentions:** *INN stem*
**Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/5/5/2`
**May also cite:** `TMM/Part29/5/5/6~1`

**What a good answer looks like.** Must distinguish the fact that a stem is listed from the conclusion that a ground arises, because the Manual makes the second turn on whether the stem appears in the mark in a meaningful way.

detail.title: Where an answer can go wrong
detail.text: The annex chunks carry no sentence context at all, so a retrieval system can return a correct hit that tells the reader nothing.

rows.question: What has to be established before a standalone geographical reference in a trade mark is treated as likely to cause confusion?
rows.search: CQ-0009 What has to be established before a standalone geographical reference in a trade mark is treated as likely to cause confusion? examiner

detail.text: **A good answer mentions:** *geographical reference*, *surrounding circumstances*, *average consumer*
**Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/9/9/3~1`
**May also cite:** `TMM/Part29/9#1`, `TMM/Part29/9/9/4`

**What a good answer looks like.** Must present the criteria as a set that must all be met, must include the mitigating-elements criterion, and must not compress them into a single likelihood judgement.

detail.title: What the stored query does not establish
detail.text:
Returns the elements the Manual states as required, with the sentence stating each. It does not weigh them, and it does not say whether they are made out on any set of facts — that is the decision maker's evaluative judgement and stating it is PU-0001. Note GR-0008's own note: `requiresElement` reads plausibly and, on that record, says the wrong thing.

Every stored query carries a line like this. A query that returns a neat table always looks like an answer, and this is where it says what it has not proved.

rows.question: Why was no section 43 ground raised for BALI on bras, when one was raised for SHETLAND on clothing?
rows.search: CQ-0010 Why was no section 43 ground raised for BALI on bras, when one was raised for SHETLAND on clothing? examiner

detail.text: **A good answer mentions:** *reputation*, *geographical origin*, *purchasing decision*
**Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/9/9/3~1`
**May also cite:** `TMM/Part29/9/9/3~2`
**What a good answer looks like.** Must attribute the difference to the reasons the Manual gives, and must not offer a general rule about place names that the Manual does not state.

detail.title: Where an answer can go wrong
detail.text: Both examples are stated in the Manual with their outcomes. Answering from the citations alone is impossible — no decision text exists in the programme (Q-11).

rows.question: Does a descriptive term inside a trade mark trigger section 43 on its own?
rows.search: CQ-0011 Does a descriptive term inside a trade mark trigger section 43 on its own? examiner

detail.text: **A good answer mentions:** *descriptive matter*, *real and tangible danger*, *specification*
**Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/4#1`, `TMM/Part29/3#1~1`
**May also cite:** `TMM/Part29/2/2/1~1`

**What a good answer looks like.** Must answer in the negative and state the condition under which it does arise — a connotation directly contradicted by the specification. Must keep the two worked PLATYPUS examples distinguishable rather than merging them.

detail.title: What the stored query does not establish
detail.text:
Returns what the Manual states, and the statement is a negative one — the `doesNotGiveRiseTo` edges. This is the case a word-overlap system gets backwards: asked to support "descriptive matter gives rise to a section 43 ground", it finds the passage that says the opposite and cites it (GX-0013). The qualification in the sentence is part of the answer and must travel with it.

Every stored query carries a line like this. A query that returns a neat table always looks like an answer, and this is where it says what it has not proved.

rows.question: Is the connotation in this trade mark strong enough to warrant a ground for rejection?
rows.search: CQ-0012 Is the connotation in this trade mark strong enough to warrant a ground for rejection? examiner

detail.text: **A good answer mentions:** *presumption of registrability*, *obvious, direct and immediate*
**Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/2/2/4`, `TMM/Part29/3#1~2`
**May also cite:** `TMM/Part29/1#1`

**What a good answer looks like.** Must decline to reach the conclusion, must state the considerations the Manual says bear on it, and must surface the presumption of registrability — that where there is doubt a connotation exists, the ground should not be raised.

detail.title: Where an answer can go wrong
detail.text: This question is deliberately one the system must not answer. It is bounded by PU-0001 and PU-0004.

detail.title: What the stored query does not establish
detail.text:
This query returns considerations and stops, which is the whole point of it. The question is an evaluative judgement for the decision maker on the material before them; PU-0001 and PU-0003 are the two outputs that answer it, and the last column names the prohibitions this question provokes. A row count here is not a score.

Every stored query carries a line like this. A query that returns a neat table always looks like an answer, and this is where it says what it has not proved.

rows.question: At what point in time is the marketplace assessed when deciding whether a sign is likely to deceive or cause confusion?
rows.search: CQ-0015 At what point in time is the marketplace assessed when deciding whether a sign is likely to deceive or cause confusion? examiner

detail.text: **A good answer mentions:** *current marketplace*, *priority date*
**Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/3/3/2`
**May also cite:** `TMM/Part29/3/3/4`, `TMM/Part29/6#1~2`
**What a good answer looks like.** Must keep the currency of the Manual text and the currency of the market separate, and must not present one as evidence about the other.

detail.title: Where an answer can go wrong
detail.text: 29.6 asks how well known a person is "as at the priority date", while 29.3.2 asks about the current marketplace. Whether those are the same moment is a legal reading, not a drafting inconsistency to be smoothed over.

detail.title: What the stored query does not establish
detail.text:
Returns the Manual's statement about *which* marketplace is assessed. It does not answer "what did the Manual say on «date»" — that is a different question, it is marked out of scope in the pilot scope draft, and the snapshot cannot support it: there is no corpus-level version stamp and the amendment history is the upstream repository's git history (Q-05). CQ-0014 is the record that carries that limitation.

Every stored query carries a line like this. A query that returns a neat table always looks like an answer, and this is where it says what it has not proved.

rows.question: If section 43 were amended, which parts of the Manual would need reviewing?
rows.search: CQ-0017 If section 43 were amended, which parts of the Manual would need reviewing? maintainer

detail.text: **A good answer mentions:** *ground for rejection*
**Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/1#1`, `TMM/Part32A/2/4/2/4/1`, `TMM/Part32B/2/2#1`
**May also cite:** `TMM/Part20/5/5/5`, `TMM/Part12/2#1`, `TMM/Part34/5/5/2`

**What a good answer looks like.** Must reach beyond Part 29 into the Parts that apply s 43 to particular subject matter, and must distinguish material that states the ground from material that merely mentions it in a list.

detail.title: Where an answer can go wrong
detail.text: Of the chunks citing the provision, some carry the edge only because upstream read a bare "section 43" out of prose and resolved it by convention. Those are inferences, not IP Australia's assertions (Q-07).

detail.title: What the stored query does not establish
detail.text:
Reviewing effort, not reviewing outcome. A Part appears because a passage in it cites the provision, not because an amendment would change what that passage means. The `inferred` column matters: those citations are upstream reading a bare "section 43" out of prose, not a link IP Australia wrote, so a Part carried only by inferred edges is a weaker claim than its count suggests. **And it counts the passages the graph holds, which is not every passage in the corpus that cites the provision.** The graph holds what this repository has said something about (ADR-0097), so for section 43 this returns 56 of the corpus's 67 citing passages; the 11 missing ones are passages no record in either store speaks about. `tmk-recon --provision TMA1995/s43` counts all 67 off the loader and is the number to quote for corpus coverage. Before the section 43 boundary was withdrawn this query was complete for section 43 and incomplete for every other provision, because the fence was drawn around that one; it is now uniformly incomplete and says so.

Every stored query carries a line like this. A query that returns a neat table always looks like an answer, and this is where it says what it has not proved.

rows.question: The WHO has notified a new International Non-Proprietary Name. What in our practice material is affected?
rows.search: CQ-0018 The WHO has notified a new International Non-Proprietary Name. What in our practice material is affected? maintainer

detail.text: **A good answer mentions:** *International Non-Proprietary Name*, *INN stem*
**Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/5/5/1`, `TMM/Part29/5/5/4`
**May also cite:** `TMM/Part29/5/5/3`, `TMM/Part29/5/5/5`

**What a good answer looks like.** Must identify that the practice depends on an externally maintained list rather than on the Manual's own text, and must name the annex as a derived artefact that goes stale silently.

detail.title: What the stored query does not establish
detail.text:
Finds the material that depends on the external register, by the approved `dependsOnExternalSource` edges and the concepts around them. It cannot tell you whether the new INN actually affects any particular mark, and it does not include the INN stem annex — twenty-odd chunks of bare word fragments with no sentences, which GS-0007 treats as tempting wrong answers rather than as answers.

Every stored query carries a line like this. A query that returns a neat table always looks like an answer, and this is where it says what it has not proved.

rows.question: If the practice on connotation in Part 29.2 changed, what else would have to change with it?
rows.search: CQ-0019 If the practice on connotation in Part 29.2 changed, what else would have to change with it? maintainer

detail.text: **A good answer mentions:** *connotation*, *denotation*
**Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/2/2/1~1`, `TMM/Part29/3#1~1`
**May also cite:** `TMM/Part29/2/2/2`, `TMM/Part29/2/2/3`, `TMM/Part29/9/9/3~1`, `TMM/Part32A/2/4/2/4/1`
**What a good answer looks like.** Must trace the dependency through passages that use the concept without citing the passage that defines it, and must not limit itself to passages that link.

detail.title: Where an answer can go wrong
detail.text: Unresolvable internal references are dropped upstream rather than recorded (Q-08), so the absence of a link is not evidence of the absence of a dependency.

detail.title: What the stored query does not establish
detail.text:
Impact by explicit dependency: concepts whose recorded definition sources sit in Part 29.2, and the approved statements read out of those same passages. It finds what is *linked*, not what is *about* the same thing — a passage that discusses connotation without citing anything and without a gold record on it is invisible here, and that is the known shape of the gap (Q-28).

Every stored query carries a line like this. A query that returns a neat table always looks like an answer, and this is where it says what it has not proved.

rows.question: Which citations in the section 43 material point at legislation we do not hold?
rows.search: CQ-0020 Which citations in the section 43 material point at legislation we do not hold? maintainer

detail.text: **A good answer mentions:** *superseded legislation*
**Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/3/3/1~2`
**What a good answer looks like.** Must name the citation and the instrument, must state that the instrument is not held, and must not silently omit the citation from a list of authorities.

detail.title: Where an answer can go wrong
detail.text: Q-24. Only two instruments are held, so every citation to an earlier Act is unresolvable by construction rather than by error.

detail.title: What the stored query does not establish
detail.text:
Says the ref lands on nothing this corpus holds. 17 of these are TMA1995/TMR1995 — the figure `tmk-recon` reports, because recon counts only the two instruments the corpus holds. The rest name instruments held nowhere in the programme at all (the 1905 and 1955 Acts, the Plant Breeder's Rights Act, the Designs Regulations), and they are unresolvable by construction rather than by omission. It does not say the citation is wrong — s 114 of the Trade Marks Act 1905 is cited by Part 29.3.1, the Manual relies on it, and the instrument is simply not in the programme (Q-24). Some of these are the s 41 renumbering trap (Q-06). None may be repaired by guessing.

Every stored query carries a line like this. A query that returns a neat table always looks like an answer, and this is where it says what it has not proved.

rows.question: Which exact passage does that statement come from, and is it the Act or the Manual?
rows.search: CQ-0021 Which exact passage does that statement come from, and is it the Act or the Manual? examiner

detail.text: **Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/1#1`, `TMA1995/s43`
**What a good answer looks like.** Must give a passage-level citation, not a Part-level one, and must label each cited passage by authority type. An answer that cites "Part 29" has not answered.

detail.title: Where an answer can go wrong
detail.text: TMM/Part29/1#1 quotes s 43 in full, so a system can satisfy a citation check while never having opened the legislation.

detail.title: What the stored query does not establish
detail.text:
Every row is a statement about section 43 whose words were read out of a Manual passage. `authority` says practice for all of them — that is the answer, and it is the one CQ-0001's caveat warns about: the Manual quotes s 43 in full inside TMM/Part29/1#1, so a passage can look like the Act and be the Manual quoting it.

Every stored query carries a line like this. A query that returns a neat table always looks like an answer, and this is where it says what it has not proved.

rows.question: Did the Manual's authors link that section themselves, or did we work it out from the wording?
rows.search: CQ-0022 Did the Manual's authors link that section themselves, or did we work it out from the wording? maintainer

detail.text: **Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/10#1`, `TMM/Part29/1#1`

**What a good answer looks like.** Must report the extraction method and, where the citation was inferred, the certainty attached to it — and must not present a `default` resolution as though IP Australia had named the instrument.

detail.title: Where an answer can go wrong
detail.text: TMM/Part29/1#1 carries an authored link; TMM/Part29/10#1 carries a bare "s43" resolved by convention. The pair is the test.

detail.title: What the stored query does not establish
detail.text:
Answers the provenance of the *edge*, not the correctness of it. `href` is the authors' own link and is the strongest evidence this corpus has; `regex`+`default` is upstream inferring the Act from a bare "section 43"; `regex`+`ambiguous` is upstream refusing to choose an instrument, and those two rows must never be resolved here (Q-07).

Every stored query carries a line like this. A query that returns a neat table always looks like an answer, and this is where it says what it has not proved.

rows.question: Which decisions does the Manual rely on for the proposition that a connotation must arise from the mark itself?
rows.search: CQ-0023 Which decisions does the Manual rely on for the proposition that a connotation must arise from the mark itself? examiner

detail.text: **A good answer mentions:** *connotation*
**Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/3/3/3`
**May also cite:** `TMM/Part29/2/2/3`

**What a good answer looks like.** Must list the decisions at citation level and must state that the holdings are not held, rather than paraphrasing what the courts decided from the Manual's summary of them.

detail.title: Where an answer can go wrong
detail.text: The Manual's own characterisation of a decision is Manual text. Repeating it as though it were the decision is an authority conflation — PU-0002.

detail.title: What the stored query does not establish
detail.text:
The first row is the answer and it is a blank one: GR-0005 states the proposition, its passage is TMM/Part29/2/2/3, and that passage cites no decision at all. The Manual asserts it without authority on the page. The OPTIONAL is deliberate — an inner join would have hidden that by returning only the rows that happened to have cases. Citation level only. These are the decisions cited by the passage that states the proposition — no decision text exists anywhere in the programme, so "which cases interpret this test" is answerable and "what did the court hold" is not (Q-11). Reading the Manual's account of a case as the court's reasons is PU-0005.

Every stored query carries a line like this. A query that returns a neat table always looks like an answer, and this is where it says what it has not proved.

rows.question: Is that a requirement, or is it how we usually do it?
rows.search: CQ-0024 Is that a requirement, or is it how we usually do it? examiner

detail.text: **A good answer mentions:** *endorsement*, *condition of registration*
**Must cite:** `TMM/Part29/1#1`, `TMM/Part29/5/5/4`
**May also cite:** `TMA1995/s43`, `TMM/Part29/6#1~2`

**What a good answer looks like.** Must separate what the Act requires from what the Manual records as practice, including for the suggested endorsement wording, which is the Registrar's suggestion rather than a prescribed form.

detail.title: Where an answer can go wrong
detail.text: The Manual states practice; it does not bind the Registrar's discretion and it is not legislation (Q-12). Every answer in the pilot has to keep that visible, and this question tests it directly.

detail.title: What the stored query does not establish
detail.text:
The modality is the reviewer's reading, recorded on the record — never inferred from the sentence's grammar. Five approved relationships carry no modality at all and appear here with none: that blank is a reportable gap, and filling it would be exactly the guess the schema forbids (guide §5.4). `authority` is practice on every row, because every one of these sentences is the Manual's.

Every stored query carries a line like this. A query that returns a neat table always looks like an answer, and this is where it says what it has not proved.

blocks.note: Click a row for what a good answer has to contain, and for what the stored query does not prove.

blocks.text:
### Two other kinds of question

**Retrieval questions** test a generated answer over retrieved passages — whether it cites the right evidence and qualifies itself properly. **Search questions** test ranked results: a query, the passages that should come back, and the ones that are tempting and wrong. Both are held to the same standard and both wait on stages that have not been built.
